title: Variance-Adaptive Optimal Algorithm for Reinforcement Learning with MNL Function Approximation
claim: Our method accumulates far less regret and learns the optimal policy faster than competing methods as problem size grows.
layout: 4 line-plot panels in one row, shared legend, sub-captions give S and H
description: A single row of four line plots showing cumulative regret (y-axis) against the number of episodes N (x-axis, 0 to about 2750) on the RiverSwim environment. Panels (a) to (d) use increasing problem sizes: S=4, H=12; S=8, H=24; S=12, H=36; S=16, H=48. Each panel has four curves with error bars and a grid. The proposed method (VAUCB) is a solid black line that flattens out or grows slowly at the bottom. The three baselines are dashed lines: UCRL-MNL+ in red, RRL-MNL in blue, and ORRL-MNL in violet. They rise much more steeply and often leave the plot area. The legend sits in the top-left of panel (a). The eye goes to the low black curve compared with the colorful baselines. The gap widens in larger panels.
caption: Empirical evaluation of the cumulative regret on the RiverSwim environment across four pairs of state S and episode length H. We compare the proposed VA-MNL against UCRL-MNL+, RRL-MNL, and ORRL-MNL. Results are averaged over 20 repeated experiments where the lines represent mean reward and shaded regions indicate standard deviation. The proposed VA-MNL yields less cumulative regret and finds the optimal policy faster than other methods.
abstract: Reinforcement learning with multinomial logistic (MNL) function approximation has become an important framework due to its flexibility and broad applicability. While existing studies have established regret guarantees under worst-case analysis, they do not capture how performance depends on the variability of the interaction between the learner and the environment. In this paper, we develop a new theoretical analysis for MNL-based Markov decision processes that yields explicit variance-adaptive regret bounds. Our algorithm is computationally efficient and achieves the instance-wise optimal rate of regret, narrowing the gap between upper and lower bounds. Our numerical experiments validate that our method learns optimal policies more efficiently than conventional approaches.
